note: 50 questions, all one level. Built for surprise while staying guessable. Every citation points at a source retrieved during research.

questions.prompt: How much did developing countries pay to service their debts in 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: $1.4 trillion — more than six times the $212 billion the world gave in aid that year.
questions.action: Compare debt payments with total aid.

questions.prompt: How much aid did wealthy countries give in 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: $212.1 billion — and it fell 7.1% in real terms from 2023, the first significant decline in years.
questions.action: Compare $212 billion in aid with $1.4 trillion in debt payments.

questions.prompt: Aid in 2024 compared with 2023:
questions.whyCorrect: Fell 7.1% in real terms, with net flows down 9.3%. Aid is shrinking exactly when needs are rising.
questions.action: Ask why rich countries cut aid budgets.

questions.prompt: Aid as a share of donor countries' national income is:
questions.whyCorrect: 0.33% — about one dollar in every three hundred. The long-standing UN target is 0.7%, more than double this.
questions.action: Work out 0.33% of a $50,000 income.

questions.prompt: How much of their national income do developing countries spend servicing debt?
questions.whyCorrect: 3.7% of gross national income — more than eleven times what donors give as a share of theirs.
questions.action: Compare 3.7% paid out with 0.33% given in aid.

questions.prompt: How much of the $1.4 trillion debt bill was interest alone?
questions.whyCorrect: $405.3 billion in interest — up 37.1% in a single year, as global interest rates rose.
questions.action: Ask what happens to debt costs when interest rates rise.

questions.prompt: Interest payments by developing countries rose by how much in one year?
questions.whyCorrect: 37.1% — a shock caused mostly by decisions taken in rich-country central banks, not by anything borrowers did.
questions.action: Ask who sets the interest rates that affect poor countries.

questions.prompt: How much of developing countries' export earnings goes to debt service?
questions.whyCorrect: 14.7% — about one dollar in seven earned from exports leaves again immediately to pay creditors.
whyWrong: Too high, though the real burden is heavy.
questions.action: Ask what a country could build with that 14.7%.

questions.prompt: How many people use the internet?
questions.whyCorrect: 5.5 billion — 68% of humanity, up from 40% in 2015. One of the fastest global changes ever measured.
questions.action: Ask what share of your school has internet at home.

questions.prompt: What share of the world is online?
questions.whyCorrect: 68% in 2024, up from 40% in 2015 — meaning about 2.6 billion people are still offline.
questions.action: Calculate how many people 32% of the world is.

questions.prompt: Internet use in sub-Saharan Africa is:
questions.whyCorrect: 37% — barely half the global 68%. The digital divide follows the same map as almost every other SDG gap.
whyWrong: Far too optimistic for the region.
Close to the global figure, not the regional one.
questions.action: Compare 37% with the world's 68%.

questions.prompt: 70% of men are online. What share of women are?
questions.whyCorrect: 65% — a five-point gender gap that persists worldwide, driven by cost, safety concerns and social restrictions.
whyWrong: The gap is five points, not thirty.
questions.action: Ask what stops a woman getting online in some countries.

questions.prompt: Internet use went from 40% in 2015 to:
questions.whyCorrect: 68% in nine years — 28 percentage points, or roughly 2.6 billion more people connected.
questions.action: Ask what you did online today that was impossible in 2015.

questions.prompt: What share of world exports come from the least developed countries?
questions.whyCorrect: 1.1% — the 44 poorest countries, holding around 14% of the world's people, sell about one hundredth of its exports.
questions.action: Compare 1.1% of exports with their share of world population.

questions.prompt: Landlocked developing countries' share of world exports is:
questions.whyCorrect: 1.2% — barely more than LDCs. Having no coastline adds cost and delay to every single shipment.
questions.action: Trace a landlocked country's route to the nearest port.

questions.prompt: How much money did migrants send home in 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: $861 billion — four times the world's total aid budget, sent by individuals to their own families.
questions.action: Compare $861 billion in remittances with $212 billion in aid.

questions.prompt: How much of the $861 billion in remittances went to low- and middle-income countries?
questions.whyCorrect: $647 billion — three times the world's aid budget, arriving directly in household bank accounts rather than through governments.
whyWrong: Some flows go between higher-income countries.
questions.action: Ask why remittances reach families more directly than aid.

questions.prompt: Global foreign direct investment in 2024 was:
questions.whyCorrect: $1.4 trillion, up 11% — but most of it flows between wealthy economies rather than to the countries that need capital most.
questions.action: Ask what foreign direct investment actually buys.

questions.prompt: How much private finance was mobilised for development in 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: $58.7 billion, alongside $303 billion in official resources — private money is growing but remains a fraction of public flows.
questions.action: Ask what makes an investor fund a project in a poor country.

questions.prompt: Official development resources in 2023 totalled:
questions.whyCorrect: $303 billion — about a fifth of what developing countries paid out in debt service that year.
questions.action: Divide $1.4 trillion by $303 billion.

questions.prompt: How many countries have statistical laws meeting international standards?
questions.whyCorrect: 159, up from 132 in 2019. Independent statistics are how any of these goals get measured honestly.
questions.action: Look up who publishes your country's official statistics.

questions.prompt: How many countries have national statistical plans?
questions.whyCorrect: 137 have a plan — but only 95 are fully funded. Plans without budgets do not produce data.
questions.action: Ask what a country cannot do without good statistics.

questions.prompt: Of 137 countries with statistical plans, how many are fully funded?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 95. Forty-two countries have written a plan to measure their own development and have no money to carry it out.
whyWrong: That's the number with plans, not funding.
Far more than five are funded.
questions.action: Ask why measuring progress is itself expensive.

questions.prompt: The long-standing UN target for aid as a share of donor income is:
questions.whyCorrect: 0.7% — agreed in 1970 and met by only a handful of countries. Actual giving is 0.33%, less than half.
questions.action: Look up which countries actually meet 0.7%.

questions.prompt: Remittances of $861 billion compared with aid of $212 billion are:
questions.whyCorrect: Migrants send home about four times what all the world's governments give in aid — the largest financial flow to developing countries by far.
questions.action: Divide $861 billion by $212 billion.

questions.prompt: Developing countries paid $1.4 trillion in debt and received $212 billion in aid. The net flow was:
options: Strongly outward — more money left than arrived
questions.whyCorrect: Debt service alone was more than six times aid received. On this measure, money flows from poorer countries to richer ones.
questions.action: Subtract $212 billion from $1.4 trillion.

questions.prompt: Principal repayments by developing countries in 2023 were:
questions.whyCorrect: $950.9 billion, plus $405.3 billion of interest — together the $1.4 trillion total.
questions.action: Add $950.9 billion and $405.3 billion.

questions.prompt: The difference between principal and interest on a debt is:
options: Principal is the borrowed amount; interest is the extra cost of borrowing it
questions.whyCorrect: Principal reduces what you owe; interest doesn't. Interest rising 37.1% means far more money spent without reducing the debt at all.
whyWrong: They are distinct components of a repayment.
Payments usually cover interest and principal together.
questions.action: Look at how a loan repayment splits into two parts.

questions.prompt: 2.6 billion people still offline mostly lack:
options: Affordable devices, data and in some places any coverage
questions.whyCorrect: Coverage reaches 96% of people, so the barrier is mostly cost — the device and the data, not the signal.
whyWrong: Demand is high wherever access becomes affordable.
Electricity matters, but affordability is the main barrier.
questions.action: Price the cheapest smartphone and monthly data where you live.

questions.prompt: LDCs holding 1.1% of world exports while home to about 14% of people means:
options: They're excluded from the trading system that drives global growth
They export more than their share
questions.whyCorrect: A thirteenfold gap between population share and export share. Trade is the main engine of growth, and the poorest countries barely participate.
whyWrong: Their export share is far below their population share.
Trade is heavily concentrated in richer economies.
questions.action: Ask what a country needs before it can export.

questions.prompt: Interest costs rising 37.1% in one year hurts development because:
options: Every extra dollar of interest is a dollar not spent on schools, clinics or roads
questions.whyCorrect: Debt service competes directly with public services. Many countries now spend more on interest than on health or education.
whyWrong: A $405 billion interest bill has enormous opportunity cost.
Interest is a cost, not a source of funding.
questions.action: Compare your country's debt interest with its health budget.

questions.prompt: Aid falling 7.1% in 2024 matters most because:
options: It happens as conflict, debt and climate costs all rise together
questions.whyCorrect: Conflict deaths rose 40%, displacement hit 123 million, and debt service hit $1.4 trillion — while the aid response shrank.
whyWrong: Aid is 0.33% of donor income against a 0.7% target.
questions.action: Ask what a donor country cut to reduce its aid.

questions.prompt: The five-point internet gender gap (70% men, 65% women) is largest in:
options: Lower-income countries, where the gap is far wider than the global average
questions.whyCorrect: The global gap is five points, but in poorer regions cost, safety and social restrictions widen it considerably.
whyWrong: The gap varies substantially by region.
questions.action: Ask what a phone gives someone that they lose without one.

questions.prompt: Only 95 of 137 statistical plans being funded means:
options: 42 countries plan to measure their development but cannot pay to do it
questions.whyCorrect: Censuses and surveys cost real money. Unfunded plans mean countries — and the world — flying blind on their own progress.
whyWrong: A national census costs tens of millions.
questions.action: Look up when your country last ran a census.

questions.prompt: $647 billion in remittances to developing countries reaches families:
options: Directly, without passing through any institution's priorities
questions.whyCorrect: Remittances go straight to households, which is why they're so effective — and why the 6.7% transfer fee matters so much.
whyWrong: They are gifts to family, not loans.
questions.action: Ask what a family spends remittance money on first.

questions.prompt: Global FDI of $1.4 trillion rising 11% mostly benefits:
options: Economies that already have infrastructure, skilled workers and stable rules
questions.whyCorrect: Investors go where returns are safest — which means capital flows toward places that already have capital, not toward the greatest need.
whyWrong: LDCs receive a tiny share of global FDI.
FDI drives significant growth where it lands.
questions.action: Ask what an investor checks before building a factory abroad.

questions.prompt: Statistical laws meeting standards rose from 132 to 159 countries. This matters because:
options: Independent statistics make it harder for a government to hide bad results
questions.whyCorrect: A statistics office that can't be overruled produces numbers a government may not like — which is exactly what accountability requires.
whyWrong: Independence is the foundation of credible measurement.
Every SDG target depends on measurement.
questions.action: Ask who could change an inconvenient official statistic.

questions.prompt: 14.7% of exports going to debt service means a country must:
options: Earn foreign currency mainly to repay creditors before importing what it needs
questions.whyCorrect: Debt is usually owed in foreign currency, so exports must cover repayments first — before medicine, fuel or food imports.
whyWrong: Borrowing is a choice, not automatic.
Exports continue; a share of earnings is committed.
questions.action: Ask why debts owed in dollars are riskier.

questions.prompt: Which flow to developing countries is largest?
questions.whyCorrect: Remittances dwarf every other flow — ordinary workers abroad send home four times what all governments give in aid.
whyWrong: Aid is a quarter the size of remittances.
Mobilised private finance is the smallest of the three.
questions.action: Rank the three flows by size.

questions.prompt: Sub-Saharan Africa at 37% online while the world is at 68% means:
options: The region is roughly a decade behind on connectivity
questions.whyCorrect: 37% is close to the world's 2015 level of 40% — the region is about where everyone else was nine years ago.
whyWrong: It has the lowest connectivity of any region.
questions.action: Compare 37% today with the world's 40% in 2015.

questions.prompt: Why is Goal 17 different from the other sixteen?
options: It's about money, data and cooperation — the means to achieve every other goal
questions.whyCorrect: Goal 17 is the machinery: finance, trade, technology and statistics. Without it, the other sixteen have ambitions but no engine.
whyWrong: Every other goal depends on it.
It has 19 targets, more than most goals.
questions.action: Pick another goal and name what Goal 17 supplies it.

questions.prompt: Donors give 0.33% of income while borrowers pay 3.7% of income in debt service. That ratio is roughly:
questions.whyCorrect: Poorer countries pay out about eleven times more of their income than rich countries give — the clearest single number in Goal 17.
whyWrong: The flow runs against developing countries.
The imbalance is more than tenfold.
questions.action: Divide 3.7 by 0.33.

questions.prompt: Internet access rising from 40% to 68% in nine years is:
options: One of the fastest technology adoptions in human history
questions.whyCorrect: About 2.6 billion people connected in under a decade — faster than electricity, telephones or literacy ever spread.
whyWrong: It is exceptionally rapid by historical standards.
questions.action: Ask how long electricity took to reach two thirds of the world.

questions.prompt: LDCs and landlocked countries hold about 1.1% and 1.2% of exports. This suggests:
options: Being poor and being landlocked are separate but similar barriers to trade
questions.whyCorrect: Poverty and geography each independently lock countries out of world trade — and some countries face both at once.
whyWrong: The groups overlap but are not identical.
Having no coastline adds major cost to every shipment.
questions.action: Find a country that is both an LDC and landlocked.

questions.prompt: Aid falling 7.1% while debt service hits $1.4 trillion creates:
options: A squeeze where less comes in exactly as more goes out
questions.whyCorrect: Both flows moved the wrong way at the same time — the core reason many countries are cutting health and education budgets right now.
whyWrong: It directly reduces money available for services.
questions.action: Ask what a government cuts first under a debt squeeze.

questions.prompt: $58.7 billion in mobilised private finance versus $303 billion official means:
options: Private money is growing but still a fraction of public development finance
questions.whyCorrect: About one private dollar for every five public ones. Hopes that private capital would fill the SDG funding gap have not yet materialised.
whyWrong: Official flows are five times larger.
questions.action: Ask what would attract more private money to development.

questions.prompt: Which Goal 17 indicator improved most clearly?
questions.whyCorrect: Connectivity is the standout success. Aid fell 7.1% in 2024 and debt service reached a record $1.4 trillion.
whyWrong: Debt service hit a record high.
questions.action: Ask what made internet access spread so fast.

questions.prompt: Good statistics matter to the SDGs because:
options: Every target has an indicator, and unmeasured progress cannot be verified or funded
questions.whyCorrect: All 17 goals rest on measurement — which is why 42 unfunded national statistical plans is a bigger problem than it sounds.
whyWrong: The entire framework depends on measurement.
questions.action: Pick a goal and find the indicator used to track it.

questions.prompt: The 'partnership' in Goal 17 mainly means:
options: Countries, companies and institutions cooperating on finance, trade, technology and data
questions.whyCorrect: No country can deliver the goals alone — debt, trade rules, climate and technology all cross borders by definition.
whyWrong: Competition alone doesn't deliver shared goals.
Even the largest donors give a fraction of what's needed.
questions.action: Name one problem your country cannot solve alone.

questions.prompt: The single most important Goal 17 number is:
options: $1.4 trillion in debt service against $212 billion in aid
questions.whyCorrect: Developing countries pay out more than six times what they receive in aid. Until that reverses, the other sixteen goals lack their funding.
whyWrong: Important, but not the binding constraint.
Significant, but mostly flowing between rich economies.
questions.action: Look up what 'debt relief' has achieved in the past.
